## Segmental duplications drive NAHR

:::{.center}
:::{.small}

- Segmental duplications (SDs) recruit NAHR
- ~5% of human genome
- High identity (>~95%)
- Large (>~10kbp)

:::

## NAHR elements and risk

<br>

:::{.small}
:::{.center}

| Homologous element | Min. Seq. identitiy | Min. length | 
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Segmental duplication (SD) | 90% | 1kbp |
| Long interspersed nuclear element (LINE) | 96% | smaller than 1kbp |
| Human endogenous retro virus (HERV) | 93% | 3kbp | 

<br>


- Risk $\propto$ length & sequence identity
- Risk $\frac{1}{\propto}$ distance between elements

:::
:::

::: notes

citation? probably one of the SV mech papers

:::

## NAHR summary

<br>

:::{.center}

- Recombination at homologous, but non-matching loci
- Breakpoints have large homology
- Example: Smith-Magenis syndrome
- Relatively high reurrency

:::

## Chronic myeloid leukemia fusion

![](./img/dup-trp.inv-dup.png){fig-align="center"}

## NHEJ summary

<br>

:::{.center}

- Imperfect repair of double strand DNA break
- Minimal homology at breakpoints
- Example: BCR-ABL1 fusion CML
- *Usually* low recurrency

:::

## Temple syndrome

:::{.center}

<br>

- BIR SV: CHR 14 DUP-TRP/INV-DUP
- Symptoms
  - Intellectual disabilities
  - Early onset puberty

:::

## BIR summary

- Replication template switching due to microhomology
- Breakpoints show microhomology
- Example: Temple syndrome; CHR 14 DUP-TRP/INV-DUP
- Low recurrency

Template switching during replication

## Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease

<br>

:::{.center}

- Mechanism: CHR X DUP; PLP1 gene
- Symptoms:
  - Involuntary movements
  - Developmental delays
:::

## FoSTeS summary

:::{.center}

<br>

- Template switching from one replication fork to another
- Breakpoints have microhomology
- Example: Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease
- Low recurrency

:::

## SV mechanisms

:::{.small}
:::{.center}


| Mechanism | When | Recurrency | Breakpoint homology | Ex. pathology |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| NAHR | Recombination | Relatively high | Large | Smith–Magenis syndrome; DEL on CHR 17, RAI1 gene |
| NHEJ  | Repair | Low | None or small | Chronic Myeloid Leukemia; FUSION of BCR-ABL genes |
| BIR | Replication | Low | Small | Temple syndrome; DEL on CHR 14 |
| FoSTeS | Replication | Low | Small | Pelizaeus-Merzbacher; DUP CHR X, PLP1 gene | 

:::
:::

::: notes

- NAHR pathology: Mechanisms underlying structural variant formation in genomic disorde
- BIR pathology: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41594-025-01644-z#Sec5 table1
- NHEJ pathology: Distinct pattern of genomic breakpoints in CML and BCR::ABL1-positive ALL: analysis of 971 patients
- FoSTeS pathology: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2685756/

:::


## SV mechanism research gaps

<br>

:::{.center}

- Calling *dependent* SVs
- Calling SVs using sequencing and mechanism models jointly
- Which mechanisms are most frequent?
- Association of mechanisms and pathologies

:::

## Dependent SVs and mechanisms

:::{.center}
:::{.small}
- A single NHEJ event may produce multiple SVs
- NAHR rarely produces insertions
- Breakpoint sequence could rule out SV dependence
  - E.g., INS+DEL with large homology at DEL breakpoints
:::


![](./img/nhej.webp){fig-align="center" width="75%"}

## Complexity of 1bp context SNVs

:::{.center}

<br>

- gnomAD considers SNVs with 1bp context
  - A**C**G -> A**A**G OR A**T**G OR A**G**G
- $4^3=64$ possible 3-mers
- 3 possible SNVs per 3-mer
- Total 3-mer SNVs is $64\cdot 3=192$



:::

## MAPS

:::{.center}
:::{.small}

- MAPS: Mutability adjusted proportion of singletons
- Aggregate singletons within SNV functional classes (e.g., pLoF or missense)
- MAPS $\approx$ Observed singleton prop. $-\text{ }f$(expected singleton prop.)
- MAPS > 0: more singletons observed than expected
<!-- - Expected: derived from non-coding regions, weighted by mutation rate (freq.) -->

![](./img/maps.png){fig-align="center" width="30%"}

:::
:::

## LOEUF

:::{.small}
:::{.center}

- LOEUF: Loss-of-function observed expected upper bound fraction
- Goal: mesaure intolerance to pLoF
- Approach: score genes by pLoF SNV proportion
- Metric: #Obs. pLoF SNVs / #Exp. pLoF SNVs; take upper bound CI

![](./img/loeuf-ex.png){fig-align="center"}

:::
:::

## SV SNP LD

:::{.center}
:::{.small}

- **LD**: linkage disequilibrium
  - $r^2 \approx 1 \rightarrow$ non-random co-occurence
  - $r^2 \approx 0 \rightarrow$ random co-occurence
- Here, LD measured for SVs and nearby SNPs

:::

## SV partial element overlap

- Log enrichment: $<0 \rightarrow$ less overlap than expected
- RVIS: residual variation intolerance score (functional variant intolernace)
  - $\uparrow RVIS \rightarrow$ $\uparrow$ variant tolerance

![](./img/1kg_sv_sr-2ab.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- left: important elements less constrained for DELs 
- left: higher VAF -> lower chance of element overlap
- right: DELs are usually more constrained than other SV types

## LD of lead eQTL SNPs and SVs

:::{.small}
:::{.center}
- Hypothesis: sig. GWAS SNPs associated with SVs
- Denom: # expected SVs in LD with lead eQTL
  - Swap SV into another SV region with similar properties (e.g., VAF)
  - Restrict LD search space to +/- Xbps from TSS
  - Constrain haplotype length ($r^2$ [$\downarrow r^2 \rightarrow \uparrow$ haplotype len.])
  - Is lead eQTL SNP in haplotype length? (yes $\rightarrow+1$)
:::
:::

:::notes
- When haplotype length is constrained, # SVs in LD with lead eQTL SNP greater than expected
- The association of lead eQTL SNPs and SV is more likely the large the SV
- Yes, it's possible that traits associated lead eQTL SNPs may actually explained by SVs
:::

![](./img/1kg_sv_sr-2e.png){fig-align="center"}

## Long read (LR) depth and size

:::{.center}
:::{.small}
- ~16.9x median coverage
  - $\uparrow$ coverage $\rightarrow$ $\uparrow$ sensitivity to mosaic variants
- ~20.3kbp median read length
  - 100x larger than typical short-read
  - SVs can be contained in a single read
- LR is single-end, not paired-end
:::
:::

![](./img/1kg_sv_lr-1b.png){fig-align="center"}

## Augmented graph SV analysis

:::{.center}

1. Align to 3 different references (GRCh38, CHM13, and HPRC)

:::{.small}
- Linear: GRCh38 and CHM13
- Graph: HPRC

## Genotype v haplotype

:::{.center}
:::{.small}
- Genotype: which alleles present and how many?
  - Ex: A/A homozygous SNP at CHR4:123456bp $\rightarrow$ genotype = "1/1"
- Haplotype: which alleles physically linked on singular chromosome?
  - Ex: SNPs at bp 4 (C>A) & 7 (A>C)  are "phased" to same physical chromosome
:::

## SV sub-classes

:::{.center}
:::{.small}

- Classes resolved by SV annotator (SVAN)
- VNTR: variable number tandem repeat
- ALU: ~300bp mobile element

![](./img/1kg_sv_lr-3a.png){fig-align="center"}

:::
:::

::: notes
- VNTR is most common SV class for both DEL and INS
- DEL would remove some section of tandem repeats
- INS would add tandem repeats
- High MAF suggests these variants are not only common in magnitude, but shared across individuals
- Aside from VNTR, most other SV classes have low AF
:::

## L1 transduction activity

:::{.center}
:::{.small}
Transduction: element is copied and inserted elsewhere
:::

![](./img/1kg_sv_lr-3a-l1.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}
![](./img/1kg_sv_lr-4a.png){fig-align="center" width="60%"}

:::

:::notes
- L1: mobile element w/ characteristic ~6kbp length. includes a repeat region
- Takeaway: some mobile elements are more active than others and adjancent seq copied along is biased to the origin of element
- Tail transduction bias except for 3rd origin loci
- Not in GRCh38 nor CHM13 means it was in the graph genome
- Takeaway 2: Prior reports have many of these elements as "non-hot"/inactive, but they seem pretty active here
:::

## SVA transduction activity

:::{.center}
:::{.small}

![](./img/1kg_sv_lr-3a-sva.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}
![](./img/1kg_sv_lr-4b.png){fig-align="center" width="50%"}

:::
- SVAs are about 2-3kbp length elements
- Within element, there is bias for head/tail transduction, but across elements is well-distributed
- Greater reference agreement compared to L1 activity
- Subfamily is more entropic than L1
:::

- Leverage mechanistic models during call process rather than post-hoc annotation

## Missing driver investigation

:::{.center}
- 4/181 driver-free samples had >5% normal contamination
- DeTiN tool re-analyzed and found drivers
:::

![](./img/pcawg-3abc.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Takeaways: i) some samples' drivers were rescued after addressing tumor-in-normal contamination (a)
- Takeaways: 2) for TERT-sensitive cancers many samples depth and purity was estimated insufficient to detect TERT mutations (bc)
- a) contamination measured by variant allele frequency difference in tumor and normal
- b) Estimated mutation detection sensitivity given purity and depth
- Again, this was only done for samples w/o drivers
- c) TERT detection sensitivity in cancers where TERT is commonly mutated

:::

## SV types

![](./img/pcawg_sv-1.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- "cut/copy" -> loss/gain in copy number
- "simple/complex". complex usually has >2  breakpoints
- SVs worth discussing
  - local n-jump: DUPs and INVs
  - Cyclic template INS: copy number gains with shared-chaining breakpoints
:::

## SV tumor frequency

![](./img/pcawg_sv-2.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Takeaway a): Complex/unclassified SVs were typically most abundant, ii) DEL and tandem DUP were frequent simple types, and iii) some cancers with only a few samples had highest SV count (top value per subplot is # samples)
- a) subpanels sorted by total SV count
- Takeaway b): Esophagal cancers had a lot DEL, Tandem DUP, and complex SVs. And DELs dominanated highest SV count samples of Ovary
- The majority of this paper is describing a few categories of complex SVs
:::

## Template insertion SVs

![](./img/pcawg_sv-3abc.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- a) Cycle: the sequence of SV breakpoints returns to source and the source copy is also gained
- b) Chain: sequence of gains, but no return to source
- c) Bridge: same as cycle, but the source copy is not gained (neutral)
- Sequence path is resolved purely by breakpoints
- Q: how do we know breakpoint chains are not just due to hotspot regions?
:::

## Liver TERT cycles

![](./img/pcawg_sv-3de.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Hypothesis: TERT amplification and inc. telomere resistance may be due to these template insertion cycle events
:::

## Local n-jumps

![](./img/pcawg_sv-4ab.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Local n-jumps result in a copy # gain with an inverted segment
- Takeaway: high counts of various jump types in different cancers
:::

## Bimodal size distributions

![](./img/pcawg_sv-5ab.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Takeaway: DEL and template INS SVs concentrate at two modes: 1kbp and 100kbp
- 1kbp SVs may be due to mobile elements like L1 or SVA
- 100kbp is quite large and not easily explained by mobile elements
:::

## SV properties

![](./img/pcawg_sv-5c.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Takeaway: DEL and DUP often have opposite median shifts
- Takeaway 2: small DELs left less likely than random, but large DELs more likley than random w.r.t gene regions
- star: means significant KS hypothesis test (not-uniform)
- LAD: lamine association domain: associated with nuclear envelope management
- Compared with quantile distribution of random SV placement
:::

## Breakpoint microhomology

![](./img/pcawg_sv-5d.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Takeaway: smaller breakpoint homology was more likely
- Unclear if peaks occured at bp sizes > 50 which might be due to mobile elements

## Breakpoint element enrichment

![](./img/pcawg_sv-5e.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Takeaway 1: Enrichment of transduction/repeat elements (mobile/homologous)
- Takeaway 2: Depletion of SVs connecting fragile regions and genes
:::

## SV signatures

![](./img/pcawg_sv-6a.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Takeaway: Tandem DUPs often occur with other SV types
- Takeaway: Chromoplexy events are more often cyclic events rather than chains. Meaning the source chromosome also has copy gain
- Takeaway: INVs are crucial for fold-backs (Breakage fusion bridge)
- Columns: signatures
- Rows: SV type, size, timing
- Bar: how much SV class contributes to signature
:::

## SV discovery methods

:::{.small}
:::{.center}

| Method | Advantage | Limitation |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| Karyotyping | Chromosome-level & large SV events | Low res. |
| Array CGH | Custom probes | Incomplete coverage |
| SR WGS | High res. | Small read-context & mapping issues |
| LR WGS | High res. & large read-context | Worse base pair accuracy |
| SC | Phasing | Cell sampling bias & limited tooling |
:::
:::

- Red: tumor. Gray: non-tumor
:::

## Alternative splicing variants

![](./img/pcawg_rna-2c.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Takeaway: Reverse strand Alu elements commonly involved in splicing alternative variant events. Specifically, reverse strand transductions.
:::

## Gene fusions

![](./img/pcawg_rna-3a.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Takeaway: majority of fusion calls were novel, small subset were recurrent (>1 individual)
:::

## Dual-translocation fusion

![](./img/pcawg_rna-3b.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Takeaway: fusions can occur on a chromosome non-native to either constituent gene
- Here: ETV is from CHR12 & NTRK is from CHR15, yet they are both translocated to CHR6 resulting in a fusion.
- Empirically, about 1/5 of fusions with SV evidence were of this type called "bridge fusions"
:::

## DNA & RNA alterations by tumor

![](./img/pcawg_rna-4a.png)

:::notes
- Heiarchical clustering using alteration type counts per tumor
- Takeaway i): alternative splicing variation across tumor types is extreme. Is this due to detection sensitivity or biology?
- Takeaway ii): the heterogenity across tumor types for alteration counts is high. Tumor-wise analyses may be necessary
:::

## Driver gene DNA & RNA alterations

![](./img/pcawg_rna-4d.png)

:::notes
- Driver gene is union of PCAWG and COSMIC driver genes
- Takeaway i): RNA driver gene alterations are more common (green) than DNA driver gene alterations
- Takeaway ii): Some driver genes are biased more toward DNA alterations or vice versa. Ex: TP53 tends to be driven by DNA alterations
:::

2. Splice altering variants cluster at exon-intron boundaries
3. "Bridge" fusions are relatively common
4. Driver gene bias toward DNA/RNA alterations

## Fusion benchmarking

:::{.center}
Sections

1. Fusion calling strategy and evaluation
2. Simulation eval.
3. Cancer cell line eval.
:::

## Fusion calling strategy

:::{.center}
- 18 alignment-based methods
- 5 assembly-based methods
:::

![](./img/fusion_bench-1a.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Takeaway: 2 core strategies: i) raw read alignemnt (short contigs) and ii) Transcript assembly then alignment
- Takeaway 2: the units of fusion evidence are i) discordant/spanning reads and ii) split/junction reads
- Discordant reads are specific to paired-end technology: each mate maps fully to another gene
- Split reads are evidence in single or paired-end read techs: the read partially maps to both genes
:::

## Fusion calling evaluation

![](./img/fusion_bench-1b.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Takeaway: Use classification metrics to compare tools and select parameters (e.g., min. supporting reads per call)
- Problem: full truth set is typically unknown
- Precision = TP/ \hat{P}
- Recall = TP / P
- F1 combines recall and precision
:::

## Simulated evaluation


![](./img/fusion_bench-2ab.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Takeaway a): read methods outperform the assembly methods (Trinity and Jaffa-assembly)
- Takeaway a): Most methods performed better with longer read lengths, except SOAPFuse and Fusionhunter (older tools probably tuned to older seq. tech with smaller read lens)
- Takeaway a): best performers were Arriba, pizzly, STAR-Fusion (highest auPRC)
- Takeaway b): Higher fusion expression led to higher recall
:::

## Cell line evaluation

:::{.center}
- Experimentally validated fusions from 4/60 cell lines
:::

![](./img/fusion_bench-3ab.png){fig-align="center" width="60%"}

:::notes
- Only showing fusions called by 3 or more methods here
- Takeaway a) recall highest for tools that performed best in simulated eval
- Only 1 exp. val. fusion found by single method (FusionCatcher)
- b) left VA is recall of validated fusions, bars
- b) right VA is precision of ensemble calls (intersection), blue line
- Takeaway b):  Precision asymptotes at about 10 caller agreement
- Takeaway b): recall falls off at about 11 caller agreement
:::

## Cell line evaluation

:::{.center}
- 56 cell lines
- "Wisdom of crowds" defines TP & FP
:::

![](./img/fusion_bench-4a.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Let caller agreement threshold vary from 1,...,23 and compute TP and FP for each case -> perf. dist.
- Takeaway i): again STAR-Fusion and Arriba perform the best (raw read aligners) while assembly methods perform worst (Trinity)
- Takeaway ii): Top and bottom rankings hardly vary as caller agreement threshold changes, but middle rankings do change
:::

## Runtime

![](./img/fusion_bench-4b.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Takeaway i): Pizzly, STAR, and Arriba are also fastest alongside having high classification perf.
- However, STAR 'kickstart' is no longer supported/recommended
:::

## Cell line evaluation

![](./img/fusion_bench-4d.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- At caller agreement = 7 definition of TP and FP,
- Takeaway: STAR-Fusion has both high precision and recall. Arriba is a close second
- Takeaway 2: The assembly-based mehods have high precision, but low recall.
:::

## Fusion benchmark summary

:::{.center}
1. Raw read mapping methods outperform transcript assembly methods
2. STAR-Fusion and Arriba are top-performers
3. Similar results for simulated and cell line evaluation
:::

## Motivation

## UCSC genome browser

:::{.center}
Sections

1. Jointly view omics annotations
2. Efficiently view different resolutions

## Genome feature comparison

![](./img/ucsc-1.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Browser is relatively old, but still useful to-date
- Why useful?
- i) Comparing multiple annotation types jointly using tracks is useful for hypothesis generation; historically, finding new human genes
- ii) Annotations can be expensive to compute. A pre-computed set of annotations accessible from web saves significant time.
:::

## Efficient variable resolution

![](./img/ucsc-7.png){fig-align="center"}

:::notes
- Hierarchical feature indexing enables fast lookup
- Features are indexed to the smallest bin that contains them
- Takeaway: Can efficiently lookup relevant subset of features in a region or that intersect another feature
:::

## UCSC genome browser summary

:::{.center}
1. Efficiently view genomic features as tracks
2. Pre-computed annotations available from web
3. Updates support various genomic file format tracks
:::

## Samplot

:::{.center}
Sections

2. VCF support

## DEL

:::notes
- Takeaway: samplot can enables rapid verification of SV events
- Uses tracks to view multiple forms of SV evidence
- Track 1: short-read seq alignments
- Alignment tracks directly show SV evidence at high resolution
  - Connected squares are discordant paired-end reads
  - Dashed lines are split reads
  - Grey background distribution is coverage (reads aligned per base)
- Track 2: PacBio long-read seq alignments
- Track 3: Repeat annotation
- Track 4: Gene annotation with exons
:::
